passage: Twenty-year-old Valentina joined the vigil in the town square at dusk, holding a small candle in a paper cup. Hundreds of people had come to remember a teacher from the university who had died. Nobody gave a speech at first. Someone began to sing a quiet song, and voices joined in, some off-key. Diego, standing beside her, placed a white flower at the foot of the lamp post. Valentina did the same. She had no words for how heavy her chest felt, but lighting the candle, singing along and placing the flower gave the feeling a shape. When the crowd bowed their heads together, Valentina found that her own shoulders had dropped.

qa.q: What did Diego place at the foot of the lamp post?
qa.a: Diego placed a white flower at the foot of the lamp post.

qa.q: What was Valentina feeling in the square, and how do you know?
qa.a: Valentina felt a heavy sadness she had no words for, and the dropped shoulders at the end suggest the shared acts eased it.

qa.q: What choice did Valentina make in the square that helped, and why?
qa.a: Valentina lit the candle, sang along and placed a flower as the others did, and doing the same acts as everyone gave a shape to a feeling that had no words.

qa.q: What might the people who sang off-key have been feeling?
qa.a: They may have been more concerned with joining in than with sounding right, so singing together was more important than the tune.

grounding: A young adult takes part in a vigil and finds comfort in doing the same acts as others, since ritual gives shape to feelings without words.

passage: On the lawn of the college, the physics department held a memorial for Professor Mathur, who had taught there for thirty years. Students, staff and the canteen workers stood in a semicircle. A lamp was lit, and one by one people stepped forward to place a marigold at the photo. Jaya waited in line, hands cold. Zeenat, next to her, whispered a prayer in her own tradition. The silence lasted a full minute. Jaya, who had not cried when she heard the news, felt her eyes fill as she set down her flower. Later, in the queue for tea, nobody explained anything, but people stood close together, and Jaya found she could breathe again.

qa.q: How many years had Professor Mathur taught at the college?
qa.a: Professor Mathur had taught there for thirty years.

qa.q: What did Jaya feel as she placed the flower, and why only then?
qa.a: Jaya felt a wave of grief as her eyes filled, though she had not cried at the news; the shared act of placing the flower seems to have released it.

qa.q: What could Jaya do when the ceremony ends if sadness comes back later?
qa.a: Jaya could stay near people who were there, talk about the professor and take part in any further small remembrances.

qa.q: How might Zeenat's prayer in her own tradition sit beside Jaya's own way of mourning?
qa.a: Zeenat seems to grieve in a personal way while standing shoulder to shoulder with everyone, showing shared ritual can hold different traditions.

grounding: A young adult takes part in a memorial and finds comfort in doing the same acts as others.
